Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

vignette:
Margaret had been a homemaker for most of her adult life, raising three children alongside her husband of thirty-one years, Dale, in a small house in rural Ohio. When Dale was killed in a car accident two winters ago - struck by a pickup truck that ran a red light on an icy December evening - Margaret was not there to witness it. She learned of it the way so many people do: a knock at the door, a uniformed officer, words that seemed to arrive from somewhere outside the ordinary world. And yet, in the weeks that followed, her mind assembled its own version of the scene with terrible fidelity. She had seen the car afterward, before she fully understood she shouldn't look. The smell of the impound lot - cold metal, engine fluid, something acrid she could not name - lodged itself somewhere beneath conscious thought, waiting.

In the months after Dale's death, Margaret found herself unable to return to work in any meaningful sense, and eventually stopped pursuing the part-time bookkeeping she had taken up after the children left home. What had once felt manageable now felt impossible to organise. Sleep became unreliable almost immediately - she would lie awake past two in the morning, then startle awake at four, heart hammering at nothing she could identify. Unexpected movement near her - a cat crossing her peripheral vision, a grandchild running into the room - produced a physical jolt of alarm that frightened her as much as it confused her. She began checking the doors and windows before bed, then again after she had already settled, then once more if she woke in the night. She had come to believe, without quite articulating it to herself, that the world had revealed itself as a place where catastrophe arrives without warning, and that vigilance was the only reasonable response.

Her memory of the event - or rather, her mind's constructed version of it - behaved in ways that deepened this vigilance. When she tried deliberately to sit with what had happened, to piece together a coherent account as her pastor had once gently suggested, the memory receded. She could not hold it. Yet without any warning, something in her surroundings could collapse the distance entirely: the smell of engine oil from a neighbour's driveway, a particular quality of winter light, and she was back at the impound lot, the cold pressing in, the smell she still could not name filling her throat. These unbidden returns arrived with a sensory completeness that deliberate recall never could, and each time they did, they left her system flooded - her body convinced, again, that something terrible was actively happening. The intrusive quality of the memory fed directly into her sense of ongoing threat, as though the past were not past at all but simply waiting to recur.

Certain things in the world had become unbearable markers. Ambulances, with their lights and their urgency, brought the full weight of that December evening back to her body before her mind could intervene. Cars with visible accident damage - she had passed one in a parking lot last spring and stood frozen for several minutes - carried the same charge. December itself had become a month she dreaded from October onward, the anniversary of Dale's death functioning less like a date on a calendar and more like a horizon she was always approaching. These triggers, once encountered, did not simply produce sadness; they reinstated the state of acute threat, so that her startle response sharpened, her sleep deteriorated further, and her checking behaviours intensified in the days surrounding them. The loop was self-sustaining: her heightened vigilance kept her scanning for the very things that destabilised her, and finding them confirmed that the scanning was necessary.

What finally brought Margaret to seek help was a conversation with her youngest daughter, who had noticed that her mother had not left the house in eleven days. Margaret told the therapist she was not sure she wanted to feel better, exactly - she was not sure that was the right way to think about it. What she most feared was that processing what happened would mean letting go of Dale in some final way. What she most hoped for, though she said it quietly, was to be able to sleep through the night again.
